title: Anatomy of a Program
summary: A program is a list of **statements** inside a **function** called `main`. They run from top to bottom. Each statement ends with `;`. Comments are notes for humans.
markdown:
## Hello World, line by line ```cpp #include // 1. bring in the tools for printing int main() // 2. the program starts here { // 3. main's instructions begin std::cout << "Hi!\n"; // 4. one instruction: print Hi! return 0; // 5. finish, and report "all went well" } // 6. main's instructions end ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `#include ` | "I want to use the input/output tools." Without it, `std::cout` does not exist. | | `int main()` | The starting point. Every program has **exactly one** `main`. | | `{` and `}` | Braces mark where a group of instructions begins and ends. | | `std::cout << "Hi!\n";` | Send the text `Hi!` to the screen. | | `std::` | "From the standard library", the toolbox that comes with C++. | | `;` | The end of an instruction, like a full stop ends a sentence. | | `return 0;` | End `main`. `0` tells the operating system that nothing went wrong. | Two words for what you just read: - A **statement** is one complete instruction. It ends with `;`. - A **function** is a named group of statements. `main` is the one that runs first. ## Statements run top to bottom ```cpp #include int main() { std::cout << "One\n"; std::cout << "Two\n"; std::cout << "Three\n"; return 0; } ``` ``` One Two Three ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR S["Start of main"] --> A["print One"] --> B["print Two"] --> C["print Three"] --> E["return 0
program ends"] ``` The computer does one statement, then the next, and never skips ahead. When a program does something unexpected, walking through it one line at a time, in order, is how you find out why. ## Comments A comment is a note for whoever reads the code. The compiler ignores it completely. ```cpp // Everything after two slashes, to the end of the line, is a comment. /* A comment between these markers can run over several lines. */ ``` > [!tip] Say why, not what > **Weak:** `lives = lives + 1; // add one to lives`. The code already says that. > **Useful:** `lives = lives + 1; // bonus life every 10,000 points`. That is something the code cannot tell you. Putting `//` in front of a line switches it off without deleting it. This is called *commenting out*, and it is handy when you are hunting for a problem. ## Spacing is for people The compiler does not care about extra spaces or blank lines. To the compiler, these are identical: ```cpp std::cout<<"Hi"; std::cout << "Hi" ; ``` People care a great deal. Indent the statements inside braces by four spaces, as every example here does, and your code will show its own structure. ## Four mistakes everybody makes | Mistake | What the compiler says | |---|---| | Forgetting a `;` | `expected ';'` (often reported on the **next** line) | | Writing `Main` or `MAIN` | No starting point found. C++ is **case-sensitive**: capitals matter. | | Leaving out `#include ` | `'cout' is not a member of 'std'` | | A `{` without its `}` | An error at the very end of the file |
ideas:
1. Write a program that prints a three-line poem.
2. Comment out the middle line with `//` and run it again.
3. Swap the order of two statements. Predict the output before you run it.

cards.q: Where does every C++ program start running?
Is `int Main()` a valid starting point?
cards.a: No. C++ is case-sensitive, so `Main` and `main` are different names.

cards.q: What does `std::` in front of `cout` mean?
cards.a: That `cout` comes from the **standard library**, the toolbox supplied with C++.

cards.q: The compiler reports a missing `;` on line 8, but line 8 looks fine. Where do you look?
cards.a: At the end of line 7. The compiler only notices the `;` is missing when it reaches the next thing.
